summaries.example: Imagine a grill. Turning the gas knob can change the gas level, which can change the flame, which can change how well meat cooks. A causal model can show these links with arrows. If we pretend the flame was set low, the model helps us work out what would happen to the meat. This is an example of asking a counterfactual question: what would have happened if things had been different?
summaries.summary: Causal models are mathematical tools for thinking about cause and effect. They describe a system using variables, such as whether a stone is thrown or whether a window breaks. Equations can show how one variable depends on others, while graphs use arrows to display possible direct causes. Probability helps describe uncertainty and patterns in data. The entry also explains counterfactuals—questions about what would have happened if something had been different—and interventions, which deliberately set a variable while leaving other causal links in place. A model can be used in two directions: it can predict results from a proposed causal structure, and it can compare possible structures with observations or experiments. Still, the conclusions depend on the model and its assumptions. Data from observations alone may not always tell us which causal direction is correct. Hidden common causes can also make two variables look connected. Thus causal modeling is both a mathematical practice and a philosophical study of how causes, probabilities, choices, and “what if” questions fit together.
key_ideas: Causal models use variables, equations, probabilities, and graphs to represent systems.
An arrow can show that changing one variable may make a difference to another.
Seeing that two things occur together is not always enough to show that one caused the other.
Interventions and carefully designed experiments can help us learn about causes.
Models can help us ask what would happen under different conditions.
summaries.why_it_matters: People want to know what will happen if they change something, not merely whether two things appear together. Causal models give scientists and decision-makers a careful way to organize that reasoning. They can clarify why experiments are useful, why hidden causes matter, and why a prediction from a model is not automatically a fact about the world. They also connect everyday questions—such as “Would this action have changed the result?”—with formal tools.

important_terms.definition: A mathematical description of how parts of a system may affect one another.
A feature that can have different values, such as “flame level” or “window breaks.”
A picture made with points and arrows that shows relationships.
A statement about what would happen if something were different.
A planned change that sets one part of a system to a chosen value.

questions_to_think_about: If two things often happen together, what else might explain their connection?
How is watching something different from deliberately changing it?
What information would you need before drawing an arrow between two variables?

summaries.example: Suppose a study finds that students who use a particular study app often earn higher grades. The correlation alone does not establish that the app causes higher grades: motivation, prior preparation, or another common cause might influence both app use and grades. A causal graph can represent these possibilities. A randomized intervention that assigns students to use the app or not aims to break the ordinary influences on app use. The resulting differences in grades can then provide evidence about the app’s causal effect, provided the model and study assumptions are appropriate.
summaries.summary: Causal models represent causal relations within an individual system or population and support inferences in both directions. Given a model, one can derive probabilities, intervention effects, and structural counterfactuals. Given statistical patterns or experimental results, one can ask which models are compatible with them. The basic formal ingredients are variables, Boolean logic, probability, and graphs. Structural equation models specify how each variable depends on its parents; an intervention replaces the equation for a chosen variable, allowing its effects to propagate forward without ordinary incoming causes. Graphs summarize this structure. In probabilistic models, assumptions about exogenous error variables yield the Markov Condition, which connects graph structure to conditional independence. Minimality and Faithfulness add further constraints, though Faithfulness is presented as a methodological assumption rather than an unquestionable metaphysical truth. If time order and other assumptions are unavailable, probability alone may leave several causally distinct graphs equally compatible. Hidden common causes complicate the picture and motivate mixed graphs. Stronger assumptions about functional form, or data from interventions, can sometimes identify more of the causal structure. The entry also applies these ideas to actual causation, decision theory, and probabilistic counterfactuals, while emphasizing that results depend on the model and on what information is available.
key_ideas: Structural equation models represent causal dependence through equations; acyclic models allow values to be calculated in an ordered way.
A DAG records qualitative causal structure, but it contains less information than the full equations and does not by itself specify functional form.
The Markov Condition links a causal graph with conditional-independence patterns in a probability distribution, but it supplies sufficient rather than necessary conditions for independence.
Without time-order information or further assumptions, observational probabilities often identify only a Markov equivalence class of graphs, not one unique causal structure.
Latent common causes require richer representations, such as acyclic directed mixed graphs with double-headed arrows.
Interventions differ from observations: observation updates what we believe about the ordinary system, whereas intervention changes the system by setting a variable.
summaries.why_it_matters: Causal reasoning is central to science, medicine, policy, and everyday choice. The framework explains why prediction from observation is not automatically intervention-based explanation, why randomized trials can be informative, and why omitted variables can mislead. It also makes philosophical questions precise: whether causation can be learned from probability, how counterfactual responsibility should be analyzed, and how an agent should distinguish evidence about an action from the action’s causal effects. Causal models do not remove uncertainty; they show which conclusions follow from which assumptions.

important_terms.definition: A mathematical model representing causal relationships among variables and supporting predictions about interventions and counterfactuals.
A function that can take different values, representing events, properties, or quantities.
A set of equations in which each variable is described as depending on its immediate causal predecessors.
A directed graph with no directed cycle; arrows represent a proposed causal structure.
A probability relation in which the occurrence of one proposition changes the probability of another.
A probability relation in which, given specified conditions, one proposition adds no probabilistic information about another.
A variable or cause omitted from the model that affects two or more represented variables.
A deliberate setting of a variable that overrides its usual causal equation while leaving other equations unchanged.

questions_to_think_about: When can an observed correlation support a causal conclusion, and what assumptions are doing the work?
Why might two different DAGs produce the same conditional-independence information?
How does conditioning on a variable sometimes block a path and sometimes reveal a connection involving a collider?
Why can additional assumptions about functional form improve causal identification?
What is the difference between asking what would happen after an actual intervention and asking what would have happened in a counterfactual case?

summaries.example: A school notices that students who bring water bottles to class often seem more alert. Does bringing water cause alertness? Maybe students who sleep well are both more likely to bring water and more likely to feel alert. A graph could show sleep as a possible common cause. If the school randomly gives some students water bottles and compares them with a similar group, that is an intervention. It changes the bottle variable instead of merely observing who chose to bring one. The result would give different evidence about causation.
summaries.summary: Causal models are tools for representing and reasoning about cause-and-effect relationships. They use variables for features that can take different values, equations for dependencies, probability for uncertainty, and graphs for a visual map of possible causal links. A model can work forward: if the structure is correct, it can predict how a system responds to a change. It can also work backward: patterns of dependence and independence in data can rule out some possible structures. But this backward reasoning is limited. Several graphs may produce the same probability patterns, especially when we do not know the time order or when a hidden common cause is possible. The entry describes directed acyclic graphs, in which arrows do not form a directed loop, and mixed graphs that can display unobserved common causes. It also explains structural equation models, where an intervention replaces the usual rule for one variable. This helps distinguish observing that X has value x from setting X to x. Counterfactuals use similar intervention ideas to ask what would have happened otherwise. The framework is applied to actual causation, causal decision theory, and the discovery of causal structure through experiments. Throughout, the answer supplied by a model depends on its assumptions; the mathematics helps make those assumptions visible.
key_ideas: Causal models can predict effects from causes and can also test which possible causal structures fit observed data.
Graphs use arrows to represent direct causal relations, while equations provide more detailed information about how variables depend on one another.
Probability describes uncertainty and can reveal independence: sometimes knowing one variable gives no extra information about another once a third variable is known.
Observation and intervention are not the same. Observing a choice may reveal its causes, while intervening deliberately changes the choice variable.
Different causal graphs can sometimes agree with the same observational data, so extra assumptions, time information, or experiments may be needed.
Questions about actual causes and “what if” cases can be difficult because backup causes may produce the same outcome.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many important choices concern effects: whether a treatment helps, whether a policy changes behavior, or whether an action would have prevented an outcome. Causal models help separate these questions from simpler questions about association. They show why experiments are powerful, why hidden factors matter, and why different philosophical accounts of causation or decision-making can disagree even when they use the same data. Learning the framework encourages careful thinking about evidence, models, and uncertainty.

important_terms.definition: A model, often using mathematics, that represents how changes in one part of a system may affect another.
A quantity or event that can have more than one possible value.
A relationship in which knowing one event changes the probability of another event.
A statement asking what would have happened under a different condition, often one that did not occur.
A deliberate change that forces a variable to take a chosen value and changes how its usual causes operate.
A diagram of variables connected by arrows; a directed acyclic graph has no arrow-path that loops back to its starting point.
A cause shared by two variables but not included in the model.

questions_to_think_about: Why does correlation by itself fail to settle which direction causation runs?
How could a hidden common cause make two events look causally connected?
Why might an arrow in a graph represent only a direct cause relative to the variables included?
How could a backup cause make it hard to decide whether an event was an actual cause?
What might an experiment reveal that a survey cannot?
